newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Britain's Major vows to combat Khyber drug trade.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major vows to combat Khyber drug trade.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major on Monday stared down the Khyber Pass, the route for 80 percent of the heroin used in Britain, and promised to work with his European partners to stop the flow of drugs.
Overlooking the route used by heavily-armed drug convoys and littered with shells fired at Pakistan's crack paramilitary Frontier Corps, Major said: "The work here is clearly vital.
"This is one of the most important drug routes, one of the most dangerous drug routes. It comes from Afghanistan through Pakistan and then on to northern Europe."
Major, who said he had come to this "wild and remote area" to see for himself what was being done, said Britain already gave cash and equipment to help Pakistan's Anti-Narcotics Force.
And he pledged: "Where we can identify a shortfall in equipment, then of course we will consider putting it in."
But Major General Fazal Ghafoor of the Frontier Corps told the British Prime Minister that despite increasing success, his men could stop only a fraction of the drugs trade.

Ghafoor told Major that last year his troops seized seven tonnes of heroin and 123 tonnes of cannabis, and destroyed 17 clandestine herion processing laboratories operating in this inhospitable tribal region on Pakistan's northwestern frontier.
But officials said this was the tip of the iceberg. Around 85 percent of the heroin consumed in Britain and Europe, and half the cannabis resin seized worldwide transits the area.

The security forces fighting the traffickers in this area still dominated by fierce tribesmen said they faced smugglers equipped with better weapons, including anti-aircraft missiles, and better transport, including all-terrain vehicles.
Shooting a local driver could launch a tribal feud against the force lasting generations, Ghafood said, and troops had to resort to trying to shoot out tyres to stop the convoys.

Major flew into the pass, the scene of some of the fiercest reversals for British soldiers during the heyday of the British empire, to a traditional reception from local tribal chiefs, who presented him with gold and white garlands.
He was driven to the lookout point in an armour-plated Mercedes flanked by jeeps bristling with weapons ranging from heavy machineguns to anti-tank rocket launchers.

Just beyond his vision, over the border in Afghanistan, lies the town of Jalalabad, where the lone survivor of a British retreat from Kabul arrived on this very day 155 years ago, the only one of the 12,000-strong expedition that had set out.
Major, facing an election in less than four months and around 20 points behind the opposition Labour party, was on the last leg of a tour that has taken him to India and Bangladesh.
Earlier, he held talks with Pakistani President Farooq Leghari and former prime minister Nawaz Sharif.

Major flies to Lahore for meetings with businessmen on Tuesday before leaving for home. On Sunday he met former premier Benazir Bhutto, dismissed by Leghari in November on disputed charges of corruption.

But he did not meet the latest entrant into Pakistan's turbulent political scene, former cricketer Imran Khan, who turned down an invitation to a reception, explaining he had to be at an election rally 100 km (60 miles) away from Islamabad.
